title: A priest at the door
translation: When something happens at a house that's doing well in the world, a death or a celebration, crowds of people come to pay their respects. And there among them is a priest, one of those who are meant to live apart from the world, sending his name in and waiting at the door. Surely he could have stayed away.
Even if he has a good reason, a priest should keep his distance from people.
original: {世|よ}のおぼえ{花|はな}やかなるあたりに、{嘆|なげ}きも{喜|よろこ}びもありて、{人|ひと}{多|おほ}く{往|ゆ}きとぶらふ{中|うち}に、{聖法師|ひじりほふし}の{交|まじ}りて、いひ{入|い}れ{佇|たたず}みたるこそ、さらずともと{見|み}ゆれ。
さるべきゆゑありとも、{法師|ほふし}は{人|ひと}にうとくてありなむ。
literal: At a house whose standing in the world is brilliant, when there is grief or joy and many people come and go to call, that a holy priest mixes among them, sends in word and stands waiting: it seems he need not do so.
Even if there is a proper reason, a priest had better be distant from people.

notes.quote: 世のおぼえ花やかなる
notes.text: おぼえ: 'reputation, favour', especially favour at court. A family that is in favour, with many people who want to stay on good terms with it.
Grief or joy: a death in the family, or a promotion, a birth, a wedding. Either way, everyone comes to call. とぶらふ covers both: to visit, to ask after someone, to offer condolences.
{聖|ひじり}: a priest who lives apart from the big temples, often as a hermit or a wandering monk. Of all priests, he has the least reason to be at a rich man's door.
いひ{入|い}る: to send a message inside through a servant, here to announce himself. Then he stands and waits to be received, like everyone else.
さらずとも: 'even without doing so', that is, he need not be there. こそ … {見|み}ゆれ: the realis form of {見|み}ゆ.
うとし: 'distant, not close'. ぬ + む: 'had better be, should surely be'. Kenkō gives the rule without explaining it; section 1 already said that a priest who throws his weight around is not impressive.
